open_questions/0.rationale:
Resolved in favour of a separate entity. The male hypomorphic phenotype is now curated as MEND syndrome (Male EBP Disorder with Neurologic defects) at kb/disorders/MEND_Syndrome.yaml, bound to MONDO:0010498.
Two distinct routes let a male with an EBP variant survive, and they predict different phenotypes. A mosaic male, or one with a null allele plus a supernumerary X, has enzyme-competent clones and presents like a female CDPX2 patient - and that male stays inside this entry. A male hemizygous for a constitutional hypomorphic allele has no competent clones anywhere but retains partial activity in all of them, giving a symmetrical, neurologically weighted phenotype rather than the Blaschko-linear, asymmetric one this entry describes. That is the split.
What changed since this question was first recorded, and both premises it rested on were wrong. This rationale previously stated that "MONDO carries only MONDO:0020603": MONDO:0010498 (MEND syndrome) exists and is the term the separate entry uses. It also treated the evidence as "a single reported family": a 2025 review tabulates seven distinct EBP alleles across four unrelated families and eight sporadic patients. Either premise alone would have been enough to reopen the question.
One factual correction to what this discussion previously asserted, because it now contradicts the MEND entry. The earlier text described the male hypomorphic phenotype as presenting "without the ichthyosis and stippling of CDPX2". That generalised from the single 2014 family, whose reported features were digital abnormalities, intellectual disability and short stature. Mild ichthyosis is documented in later MEND patients, and the MEND entry curates it. The distinction between the two disorders is the *pattern* of the skin and skeletal findings - symmetrical and often transient in MEND, Blaschko-linear with follicular atrophoderma and scarring alopecia in CDPX2 - not their presence or absence.
What remains open is not the nosology but the biology: whether the two disorders sit on one activity continuum or differ in kind. That question belongs to the sterol-to-phenotype gap recorded separately, not here.

evidence.snippet: Our results indicate that defects in sterol-delta8-isomerase cause CDPX2 and suggest a role for sterols in bone development.

open_questions/1.rationale: The enzymology of CDPX2 is settled and the sterol profile is diagnostic, but the step from either sterol abnormality to abnormal calcification of cartilage is not. The gene-discovery paper put it no more strongly than that the results "suggest a role for sterols in bone development", and that remains the state of the argument. The question is answerable in principle, because CHILD syndrome supplies a precedent: there, a topical trial separating cholesterol replacement from suppression of precursor flux showed that neither arm alone accounted for the skin phenotype. No equivalent dissection has been done for the CDPX2 skeleton, and the two mechanism edges in this entry are annotated as having unknown intermediates for that reason.

evidence.snippet: An intronic POLA1 mutation (c.1375-354A>G), causing altered POLA1 gene splicing, leads to reduced transcript and protein levels.
evidence.explanation: Names the variant and summarises the splicing and expression consequence. From the introduction of a case letter, restating the 2016 discovery work.

evidence.snippet: To date, all XLPDR cases are caused by the same recurrent intronic mutation, which results in gene missplicing.
evidence.explanation: A review by the discovering group states that the variant is shared by all known cases and acts through missplicing.

evidence.snippet: support the hypothesis of very early embryonic lethality in males with POLA1 nullisomy
evidence.explanation: A family carrying a POLA1-spanning deletion supports male lethality of complete POLA1 loss, which is why the XLPDR variant must be partial.

steps/1.description: A recurrent deep intronic POLA1 variant (c.1375-354A>G on NM_016937; c.1393-354A>G on NM_001330360.2) causes aberrant splicing and reduces POLA1 transcript and protein. The same variant is found in every genetically confirmed case. Because complete POLA1 loss appears to be lethal in males, the variant is best read as hypomorphic.

evidence.snippet: This enzyme is necessary for the synthesis of RNA:DNA primers during DNA replication and, strikingly, we found that POLA1 is also required for the synthesis of cytosolic RNA:DNA, which directly modulates interferon activation.
evidence.explanation: Places the cytosolic RNA:DNA product of POLA1 directly upstream of interferon activation.

steps/2.description: Besides priming DNA replication, POLA1 synthesises RNA:DNA hybrids in the cytosol, and these hybrids modulate the interferon response. With less POLA1 their synthesis falls, removing a brake on type I interferon induction. The nucleic-acid sensor that responds is not curated here; see the knowledge gap below.

evidence.snippet: This phenotype is reminiscent of hypomorphic mutations in MCM4, which encodes a component of the minichromosome maintenance (MCM) helicase complex that is functionally linked to Pol-α during the DNA replication process.
evidence.explanation: Links the XLPDR NK phenotype to MCM4 and explains the functional tie between MCM4 and polymerase-alpha.

evidence.snippet: We find that POLA1 deficiency leads to MCM4 depletion and that both can impair NK cell natural cytotoxicity and show that this is due to a defect in lytic granule polarization.
evidence.explanation: The experimental demonstration that MCM4 is depleted when POLA1 is deficient.

steps/3.description: POLA1 deficiency depletes MCM4, a subunit of the MCM replicative helicase. The NK-cell phenotype of XLPDR resembles that of hypomorphic MCM4 mutations, and MCM4 depletion alone reproduces the cytotoxicity defect.

evidence.snippet: Reduced POLA1 expression in this condition triggers spontaneous type I interferon expression, which can be linked to the autoinflammatory manifestations of the disease.
evidence.explanation: Summarises the interferon arm and links it to the autoinflammatory features.

evidence.snippet: Compared to healthy controls, the IFN signature was elevated although the degree moderated over time with the improvement in his chest disease.
evidence.explanation: An independent patient with a raised interferon signature, which fell as his lung disease improved.

evidence.snippet: Five of six tested ISG were slightly elevated when compared to several healthy controls but not to the extent of ISG measured in a patient with a genetically proven SAMHD1-related interferonopathy
evidence.explanation: A third patient with raised interferon-stimulated genes, and a measure of how modest the signature can be.

steps/4.description: Patient cells and blood show spontaneous type I interferon expression and raised interferon-stimulated genes. The signature varies in strength: one patient's was only slightly raised, below that of a SAMHD1-related interferonopathy, and in another it moderated as his chest disease improved.

evidence.snippet: Here we report that patients with XLPDR have reduced NK cell cytotoxic activity and decreased numbers of NK cells, particularly differentiated, stage V, cells (CD3-CD56dim).
evidence.explanation: The primary report of low NK numbers, a missing mature subset and reduced cytotoxicity.

evidence.snippet: our patient had slight NK cell cytopenia and a relative paucity of mature CD56dim NK cells in peripheral blood
evidence.explanation: Replication in an unrelated patient.

evidence.snippet: NK cell functional studies showed normal cytotoxicity and degranulation.
evidence.explanation: A genetically confirmed patient with normal NK function. The authors conclude the NK defect may not be a constant feature of XLPDR.

steps/5.description: Patients have fewer NK cells, with a selective loss of mature stage V CD3-CD56dim cells, and reduced NK cytotoxicity caused by defective lytic granule polarization. The defect is not constant: one genetically confirmed patient had normal NK cytotoxicity and degranulation.

evidence.snippet: Skewed X-inactivation patterns were detected in the mother's lymphocytes.
evidence.explanation: Direct evidence of skewed X-inactivation in a carrier.

steps/6.description: In heterozygous females, X-inactivation leaves patches of skin expressing the variant allele, giving pigmentation along the lines of Blaschko while sparing other organs. Skewed X-inactivation was shown in one carrier mother's lymphocytes. That is blood, not skin: it shows the X-inactivation pattern can be skewed in carriers, and may explain why carriers are spared systemic disease, but skin mosaicism itself has not been demonstrated.

evidence.snippet: is a rare syndrome characterized by recurrent infections and sterile multiorgan inflammation
evidence.explanation: Characterises the inflammation as sterile and multiorgan.

evidence.snippet: multiorgan involvement dominated by autoinflammatory manifestations in the eyes, the urinary tract, and recurrent infections, particularly in the respiratory tract
evidence.explanation: Names the organs affected by the autoinflammation.

evidence.snippet: XLPDR has been shown to be accompanied by profound activation of type I interferon signaling, but unlike other interferonopathies, it is not associated with autoantibodies or classical autoimmunity.
evidence.explanation: Records the absence of autoantibodies that separates XLPDR from other interferonopathies.

steps/7.description: Sterile, autoinflammatory disease of the intestine, cornea, urinary tract and airways. Unlike most type I interferonopathies it is not accompanied by autoantibodies or classical autoimmunity.

evidence.snippet: Electron microscopy showed a very high number of melanosomes and some degenerating keratinocytes.
evidence.explanation: Ultrastructural evidence of keratinocyte degeneration in affected skin.

evidence.snippet: A punch biopsy specimen from the 11-year-old showed melanophages and necrotic keratinocytes.
evidence.explanation: Necrotic keratinocytes in an affected boy's skin biopsy.

steps/8.description: Skin biopsies from both sexes show degenerating or necrotic keratinocytes and pigment dropping into the dermis, where it is taken up by melanophages. How POLA1 deficiency injures the epidermis, and whether interferon signalling is involved, has not been shown.

evidence.snippet: Skin histology showed pigmentation incontinence with numerous melanophages.
evidence.explanation: Histology of an affected boy's skin.

evidence.snippet: The histopathological features of XLPDR are similar in both sexes, including mild hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, basal hyperpigmentation, and pigmentary incontinence in the upper dermis
evidence.explanation: Summarises published histology in both sexes. From the discussion of a case report whose own patient declined biopsy.

steps/9.description: Skin histology shows pigmentary incontinence with numerous melanophages in the upper dermis, in both sexes. The finding is not specific to XLPDR.

evidence.snippet: a progressive reticulate pigmentation of the skin
evidence.explanation: The second family's males show progressive reticulate pigmentation.

evidence.snippet: mottled, muddy-brown pigmentation seen first on the inner thighs and spreading diffusely to the buttocks, trunk, and arms
evidence.explanation: The original kindred's 10-year follow-up describes where the pigmentation starts and how it spreads.

evidence.snippet: had diffuse reticulate macular hyperpigmentation with onset in early childhood
evidence.explanation: Onset in early childhood in two affected brothers.

steps/10.description: Diffuse reticulate hyperpigmentation in males, starting on the inner thighs and spreading to the buttocks, trunk and arms, with mottled or guttate hypopigmented macules interspersed. It usually appears in early childhood, sometimes after the systemic features.

evidence.snippet: In the carrier females, manifestations are apparently limited to the skin with patchy linear hyperpigmentation following the lines of Blaschko that are similar to stage III incontinentia pigmenti.
evidence.explanation: Describes the carrier-female phenotype.

evidence.snippet: On examination, there were multiple, asymptomatic, brownish macules in linear and whorled patterns over the trunk, axillae, groin, and extremities.
evidence.explanation: The distribution in an adult woman. Her diagnosis was clinical and histological, without genetic confirmation.

evidence.snippet: The sister, age 2 years, had congenital linear hyperpigmented patches involving the intertrigenous areas, but was otherwise normal.
evidence.explanation: Congenital linear pigmentation with no other findings in a sister of affected boys.

steps/11.description: The phenotype of heterozygous females: linear and whorled brown macules along the lines of Blaschko on the trunk, axillae, groin and limbs, present from infancy and resembling stage III incontinentia pigmenti. Carrier females have no systemic features.

evidence.snippet: onset in the first year of recurrent episodes of respiratory illness including pneumonia
evidence.explanation: Recurrent pneumonia from the first year in the second family.

evidence.snippet: Two died of pneumonia by three months.
evidence.explanation: Fatal infant pneumonia in the founding kindred.

steps/12.description: Recurrent respiratory infection, including pneumonia, starts in the first year of life. In the original kindred several male infants died of pneumonia.

evidence.snippet: Imaging demonstrated bronchiectasis, while gastroscopy identified chronic eosinophilic gastroduodenitis.
evidence.explanation: Bronchiectasis on imaging in a genetically confirmed boy.

evidence.snippet: Changes in the lungs were those of late-stage diffuse pulmonary fibrosis.
evidence.explanation: Autopsy finding in a 50-year-old affected man with recurrent pneumonia. A single case.

evidence.snippet: He suffered recurrent chest infections with chronic cough, clubbing, and asthma
evidence.explanation: Clubbing with chronic chest infection in a genetically confirmed boy.

evidence.snippet: One died at three months from colitis. Both remaining boys had colitis as infants
evidence.explanation: Infant colitis, including a death, in the founding kindred.

evidence.snippet: Gastrointestinal biopsies now demonstrated increased intraepithelial apoptosis and eosinophilic inflammation, most pronounced in the ascending colon, requiring systemic steroids
evidence.explanation: Histology of colitis in a genetically confirmed patient.

steps/16.description: Neonatal or infantile colitis, sometimes bloody and sometimes fatal in the founding kindred, and later inflammatory bowel disease. The first genetically confirmed patient with bowel histology had intraepithelial apoptosis and eosinophilic inflammation with raised epithelial MX1.

evidence.snippet: These included neonatal colitis, infantile diarrhea, recurrent respiratory infections, corneal dystrophy, photophobia
evidence.explanation: Infantile diarrhoea among the male manifestations in the original kindred.

evidence.snippet: the disease typically manifests in the first months of life with failure to thrive, recurrent pneumonias, persistent diarrhea in infancy, and pathognomonic diffuse hyperpigmentation and characteristic facies
evidence.explanation: Summarises the infant presentation, including persistent diarrhoea.

evidence.snippet: these boys had hypohydrosis, coarse hair with an upswept frontal hairline, failure to thrive, and chronic pulmonary disease
evidence.explanation: Failure to thrive in two affected brothers.

evidence.snippet: Both males had thrived poorly as infants but had survived.
evidence.explanation: Poor infant growth in the surviving males of the founding kindred.

evidence.snippet: The older boy also had corneal dystrophy and marked photophobia.
evidence.explanation: Corneal dystrophy with photophobia in an affected boy.

evidence.snippet: near-blindness from amyloid deposition in the cornea
evidence.explanation: Severe corneal involvement in the founding kindred. The authors put it down to amyloid, which later families did not confirm.

steps/19.description: Progressive corneal disease with opacification, reported as corneal dystrophy and in the founding kindred as near-blindness. The sources call it a dystrophy, but it is thought to be inflammatory.

evidence.snippet: developed photophobia as well as bilateral lop ears at the age of 3 months
evidence.explanation: Photophobia from 3 months of age.

evidence.snippet: photophobia, abnormal hair, developmental delay, and recurrent bronchitis
evidence.explanation: Photophobia in an unrelated affected boy.

steps/20.description: Photophobia can begin in early infancy; in one genetically confirmed boy it started at 3 months.

evidence.snippet: the other had recurrent pneumonia throughout life, a urethral stricture, inguinal herniae, and near-blindness from amyloid deposition in the cornea
evidence.explanation: Urethral stricture in an affected male of the founding kindred.

evidence.snippet: gastrointestinal inflammation, urethral stricture, failure to thrive, and characteristic upswept hair and flared eyebrows
evidence.explanation: Lists urethral stricture among the features of affected males in the Canadian kindred.

steps/21.description: Inflammatory narrowing of the urethra. It is recorded in the founding kindred and is part of the urinary tract autoinflammation.

evidence.snippet: Here we report that patients with XLPDR have reduced NK cell cytotoxic activity and decreased numbers of NK cells, particularly differentiated, stage V, cells (CD3-CD56dim).
evidence.explanation: Low NK cell numbers in patients.

evidence.snippet: NK cell count was slightly low in absolute numbers, while total B and T cell numbers were normal.
evidence.explanation: Mildly low NK count with normal T and B cells in an unrelated patient.

evidence.snippet: The relative proportion of immature CD56hi NK cells was 2-fold elevated compared to the two controls
evidence.explanation: A doubled immature NK fraction in a genetically confirmed patient.

steps/23.description: Loss of mature CD56dim NK cells, so the immature CD56bright fraction is relatively expanded.

evidence.snippet: Here we report that patients with XLPDR have reduced NK cell cytotoxic activity
evidence.explanation: Reduced NK cytotoxicity in patients.

evidence.snippet: NK cell functional studies showed normal cytotoxicity and degranulation.
evidence.explanation: A genetically confirmed patient with normal NK cytotoxicity.

evidence.snippet: we found that POLA1 is also required for the synthesis of cytosolic RNA:DNA, which directly modulates interferon activation
evidence.explanation: Establishes that POLA1 is required for cytosolic RNA:DNA synthesis, so reduced POLA1 reduces it.

edges/2.description: Reduced POLA1 lowers synthesis of cytosolic RNA:DNA hybrids.

evidence.snippet: We find that POLA1 deficiency leads to MCM4 depletion and that both can impair NK cell natural cytotoxicity
evidence.explanation: Direct experimental statement that POLA1 deficiency causes MCM4 depletion.

edges/3.description: POLA1 deficiency depletes MCM4, the MCM helicase subunit that works with polymerase-alpha during replication.

evidence.snippet: Unexpectedly, POLA1 deficiency resulted in increased production of type I interferons.
evidence.explanation: POLA1 deficiency raises type I interferon production, the consequence of losing the modulating RNA:DNA species.

edges/4.description: Loss of cytosolic RNA:DNA removes a restraint on the type I interferon response.

evidence.snippet: detected upregulated expression of MX1, a prototypic ISG-protein, in epithelial and immune cells
evidence.explanation: Shows the interferon response inside inflamed colonic tissue. The authors also saw epithelial MX1 in ordinary IBD, so it marks tissue interferon activity but does not prove it causes the inflammation.

edges/5.description: Chronic interferon signalling is linked to the sterile inflammation of the gut, eye, urinary tract and airway.

edges/6.description: Intestinal inflammation presenting as neonatal or infantile colitis and, later, inflammatory bowel disease.

evidence.snippet: multiorgan involvement dominated by autoinflammatory manifestations in the eyes, the urinary tract, and recurrent infections, particularly in the respiratory tract
evidence.explanation: Names the eye among the autoinflammatory manifestations.

edges/7.description: Inflammatory corneal disease, reported as corneal dystrophy.

evidence.snippet: multiorgan involvement dominated by autoinflammatory manifestations in the eyes, the urinary tract, and recurrent infections, particularly in the respiratory tract
evidence.explanation: Names the urinary tract among the autoinflammatory manifestations.

edges/8.description: Inflammatory disease of the urinary tract, including urethral stricture.

evidence.snippet: We find that POLA1 deficiency leads to MCM4 depletion and that both can impair NK cell natural cytotoxicity and show that this is due to a defect in lytic granule polarization.
evidence.explanation: Shows that MCM4 depletion itself impairs NK cytotoxicity, and names the cellular defect.

edges/9.description: MCM4 depletion impairs NK cell natural cytotoxicity through defective lytic granule polarization.

edges/10.description: The maturation defect shows up in blood as a low NK count.

edges/11.description: Loss of the mature CD56dim subset skews the bright/dim ratio.

edges/12.description: Defective lytic granule polarization reduces target-cell killing.

evidence.snippet: Rather, it is accompanied by marked Natural Killer (NK) cell dysfunction, which may explain the recurrent infections seen in this syndrome.
evidence.explanation: States NK dysfunction as the likely, not proven, explanation for the infections.

edges/13.description: NK dysfunction is the proposed explanation for recurrent infections in patients whose T and B cells and antibodies are normal.

edges/14.description: Pigment released from injured basal keratinocytes drops into the upper dermis.

edges/15.description: Mosaic expression in the skin produces the Blaschko-linear pattern seen in carrier females.

evidence.snippet: suggesting that those might be responsible for the hyperpigmentation
evidence.explanation: The case report's discussion proposes that the dermal melanophages and amyloid-like material cause the pigmentation, and says further study is needed.

edges/16.description: Dermal melanophages are the proposed cause of the visible hyperpigmentation. The authors present this as a suggestion.

edges/17.description: Repeated lower respiratory infection leads to bronchiectasis.

edges/18.description: Late-stage diffuse pulmonary fibrosis at autopsy in a man with lifelong recurrent pneumonia.

edges/19.description: Chronic suppurative lung disease is followed by digital clubbing.

edges/20.description: Intestinal inflammation presents as persistent diarrhoea in infancy.

evidence.snippet: Males may suffer severe gastrointestinal disorders in infancy with failure to thrive and early death.
evidence.explanation: Links gastrointestinal disease in infancy to failure to thrive.

edges/21.description: Severe gastrointestinal disease in infancy causes failure to thrive.

evidence.snippet: corneal dystrophy with severe photophobia
evidence.explanation: Pairs the corneal disease with the photophobia it causes.

evidence.snippet: We discovered that XLPDR is caused by an intronic mutation that disrupts the expression of POLA1, which encodes the catalytic subunit of DNA polymerase-α.
evidence.explanation: The gene-discovery report.

evidence.snippet: To date, all XLPDR cases are caused by the same recurrent intronic mutation, which results in gene missplicing.
evidence.explanation: All known cases share one variant.

genes/0.notes: The disease has so far shown no allelic heterogeneity. Other hypomorphic POLA1 variants cause a different disorder, van Esch-O'Driscoll syndrome, and POLA1 is also reported as an X-linked dyskeratosis congenita gene. No ClinGen gene-disease validity record for POLA1 and this disease is cached in the repository, so no validity tier is recorded. In one patient the variant arose de novo.

evidence.snippet: This patient had multiple atopic manifestations affecting eye, skin, chest, and gut, complicating the presentation of XLPDR.
evidence.explanation: The authors attribute the atopic features to the co-occurring FLG variant.

genes/1.notes: One patient, a single case report. A heterozygous FLG nonsense variant was proposed to add atopic eczema, asthma, keratitis and food allergy to the XLPDR presentation. Recorded as a modifier of presentation, not of the XLPDR mechanism itself.

evidence.snippet: treatment of the index patient was started with the JAK1/3 inhibitor tofacitinib as an immune-modulating monotherapy
evidence.explanation: The agent and treatment strategy used.

evidence.snippet: To our knowledge, this is the first XLPDR patient treated with a JAK inhibitor, associated with a clinical response without adverse symptoms or side effects on laboratory parameters.
evidence.explanation: A clinical response without side effects in the only reported treated patient.

evidence.snippet: No bacterial or opportunistic infections occurred during the first 8 months of tofacitinib treatment.
evidence.explanation: No infections on treatment, relevant because JAK inhibition is immunosuppressive in a disorder with recurrent infections.

evidence.snippet: First generation Janus kinase inhibitors including baricitinib, tofacitinib and ruxolitinib are useful for disease control.
evidence.explanation: A review of type I interferonopathies, which it says include XLPDR, supports JAK inhibitors for the group. INDIRECT because it is not XLPDR-specific.

treatments/0.description: Oral JAK1/3 inhibitor, chosen because type I interferon receptors signal through JAK-STAT. In one boy with interferon-driven colitis it was given as monotherapy (10 mg daily for 14 days, then 5 mg daily). Abdominal pain and faecal calprotectin fell, blood ISG expression tended to fall, and no bacterial or opportunistic infections occurred in the first 8 months. This is a single uncontrolled case.

evidence.snippet: There was a tendency of reduced ISG in peripheral blood when re-assessed after 8 weeks and 8 months of JAK inhibition
evidence.explanation: The interferon signature tended to fall on treatment. The authors call it a tendency; this is one patient.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: JAK inhibition blocks signalling downstream of the type I interferon receptor.

evidence.snippet: After an initial good response to mesalazine, abdominal pain re-occurred at the age of 7 years.
evidence.explanation: A transient response to mesalazine in one patient.

evidence.snippet: Gastrointestinal biopsies now demonstrated increased intraepithelial apoptosis and eosinophilic inflammation, most pronounced in the ascending colon, requiring systemic steroids
evidence.explanation: The colitis relapse needed systemic corticosteroids.

treatments/1.description: Conventional anti-inflammatory treatment for XLPDR colitis. In the one patient with documented bowel histology, mesalazine helped at first, but abdominal pain returned and systemic steroids were needed before JAK inhibition was tried.

open_questions/0.rationale: The interferon and NK-cell arms explain the inflammatory and infectious features, but no cited study links either to the skin and ectodermal phenotype. A 2022 case report says the mechanisms for pigmentation remain elusive and suggests dermal melanophages and amyloid-like material may be responsible. So the keratinocyte injury node in this entry has no upstream edge, and hypohidrosis and the facial features are not wired to any mechanism.

open_questions/1.rationale: The 2016 discovery work shows that POLA1 is needed for cytosolic RNA:DNA synthesis and that this RNA:DNA modulates interferon activation. The abstracts cited here do not name the sensor, so whether the pathway runs through cGAS-STING or another sensor is not curated. The edge from reduced RNA:DNA to interferon activation stands without a named intermediate.

open_questions/2.rationale: The founding NK study and a Swiss case found low, immature and poorly cytotoxic NK cells, but a genetically confirmed patient had normal NK cytotoxicity and degranulation, and his authors conclude the defect may not be constant. The review from the discovering group says NK dysfunction "may explain" the infections, but this has not been tested directly.
